common_name: Munger Black Raspberry (Historic Commercial Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring; Munger was, for most of the 20th century, the dominant black raspberry cultivar grown for commercial canning and freezing and remains a reliable, vigorous choice for the home patch.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and tip-prune new canes at about 24-30 inches during the summer to force branching, since black raspberries fruit on lateral shoots off last year's canes rather than on the cane tips. Munger was selected in the late 1800s and went on to become the backbone of the commercial black raspberry industry in Oregon and the Midwest for decades, prized for its productivity, vigor, and the deep, wine-dark, firm berries that hold up well to picking and processing. The flavor is intensely rich and slightly tart, excellent for jam, syrup, and baking, and the arching canes root readily wherever an unpruned tip touches soil, so stake or tip-prune to keep the planting from wandering. Remove spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to the strongest four or five per hill each spring.

common_name: Bristol Black Raspberry (Cornell Standard Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring; Bristol is a Cornell University release from the 1930s that remains one of the most widely grown black raspberries for home gardens for its large, glossy, firm fruit and vigorous, upright canes.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and tip-prune vigorous new canes in midsummer to encourage the lateral branching that carries next year's crop. Bristol was released by Cornell University in 1934 and quickly became a garden standard for its large, glossy-black, firm berries with rich, classic black raspberry flavor, produced in heavy clusters on strong, upright canes that need less support than sprawling types. It ripens in a concentrated midsummer window that makes for an efficient single harvest push, and the vigorous habit means a modest planting fills in and produces well within its second season. Watch for anthracnose in humid climates and provide good air circulation between hills; remove spent floricanes immediately after harvest to reduce disease pressure on the new canes.

common_name: Cumberland Black Raspberry (Classic Heirloom Black Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in early spring; Cumberland is an early-1900s heirloom black raspberry still grown today for its large, firm, richly flavored berries on tall, vigorous canes.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and give the tall, arching canes a simple wire support or tip-prune them at knee height in summer to keep the planting manageable. Cumberland is one of the oldest black raspberry cultivars still in commerce, long valued for unusually large, firm, deep-black berries with an intense, old-fashioned flavor well suited to jam, pie, and syrup making. The vigorous canes root at the tips wherever they touch soil, which is a fast way to propagate new plants but also means unchecked plantings will spread beyond their bed if canes aren't tipped back or trained. Remove spent floricanes after the midsummer harvest and thin to the sturdiest canes each spring for the best fruit size the following year.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; Nantahala is a North Carolina State University release bred specifically for better heat and humidity tolerance than standard red raspberries, making it one of the more realistic red raspberry options for warm Southern gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool through summer heat, since red raspberries generally struggle south of the mountains. Nantahala was bred at North Carolina State University specifically to extend red raspberry production into warmer parts of the Southeast, combining better heat tolerance with good fruit size and quality than older Northern-bred varieties typically manage in Southern gardens. It bears its primary crop on second-year floricanes in early summer, ahead of the worst heat, and benefits from consistent irrigation and a site with some afternoon relief in the hottest zone 8-9 gardens. Even with its improved heat tolerance, red raspberry remains a marginal crop in the Deep South, so gardeners in zone 9 should treat it as an experiment best sited in the coolest, most sheltered spot available.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, or set out plugs in fall in mild climates; Flavorfest is a USDA-ARS release bred for outstanding fresh-eating flavor and good disease resistance in a mid-to-late June-bearing strawberry.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown right at soil level in full sun in well-drained, well-prepared soil, and remove the first flush of blossoms in a spring-planted bed's first weeks to push energy into establishment. Flavorfest was released by the USDA in the mid-2010s from the Beltsville breeding program specifically to combine excellent, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor with good resistance to common foliar diseases and better tolerance of a range of soil conditions than many older June-bearing varieties. The large, firm, glossy red berries ripen in a mid-to-late June-bearing window and hold their flavor and size well through the peak of the harvest rather than tapering off in smaller, less flavorful late fruit. Renovate the bed after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to maintain a productive planting for several years, and mulch with straw over winter in colder parts of its range.
